theory.overview: Virtual memory is one of computing's most powerful abstractions—it gives each program the illusion of having the entire address space to itself, while the hardware and operating system secretly map these virtual addresses to physical RAM locations. This decoupling enables features impossible with physical addressing alone: memory protection (programs can't corrupt each other), efficient memory sharing (shared libraries), demand paging (running programs larger than physical RAM), and seamless multitasking. Understanding virtual memory reveals how modern operating systems create secure, stable, and efficient computing environments.

sections.title: Why Virtual Memory?
sections.content: Without virtual memory, programs directly manipulate physical addresses, leading to chaos: programs can read/write each other's memory, must be loaded at specific addresses, and can't run if they don't fit in RAM. Virtual memory solves these problems by adding an address translation layer. Each program sees a contiguous virtual address space (typically 0 to 2^64 on 64-bit systems) while the Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual to physical on every access.

benefits.isolation: Programs cannot access each other's memory
benefits.relocation: Program can run at any physical location
benefits.sharing: Same physical memory mapped to multiple processes
benefits.capacity: Programs larger than physical RAM via swapping

sections.title: Pages and Frames: The Translation Unit
sections.content: Virtual and physical memory are divided into fixed-size blocks. Virtual pages (typically 4KB, but also 2MB/1GB huge pages) map to physical page frames. The translation: virtual page number → physical frame number, with the page offset unchanged. This page-based approach makes translation table sizes manageable—a 4GB address space with 4KB pages needs only 1 million page entries (4GB/4KB), not billions of byte-level entries.

sections.title: Page Tables: The Translation Map
sections.content: Page tables store virtual-to-physical mappings. Each process has its own page table hierarchy. x86-64 uses a 4-level page table: the virtual address splits into 4 index portions (each 9 bits = 512 entries) plus offset. The CPU walks this tree: CR3 register points to top-level (PML4), which points to PDPT, which points to PD, which points to PT, which contains the physical frame number. This multi-level approach keeps tables compact—unused portions need no allocated pages.

sections.title: TLB: Translation Cache
sections.content: Page table walks are slow (4-5 memory accesses). The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) caches recent translations. On each memory access, the MMU first checks the TLB. A TLB hit completes translation in 1 cycle. A TLB miss triggers a page table walk (slow) then caches the result. TLBs are small (64-1024 entries), fully or set associative, and critical for performance. Context switches flush TLBs (or use ASIDs to avoid it).

sections.title: Page Faults and Demand Paging
sections.content: When the MMU finds no valid mapping (page not present), it raises a page fault exception. The OS handler: validates the access (if invalid, kill program with segfault); allocates a physical page if needed; loads data from disk if swapped out; updates the page table; restarts the faulting instruction. This demand paging enables running programs larger than physical memory—only actively used pages reside in RAM.

sections.title: Memory Protection and Permissions
sections.content: Each page table entry contains permission bits: Present (page in memory), Read/Write (allow writes), User/Supervisor (access ring), Execute Disable (NX bit—prevents code execution from data pages, blocking many exploits), and Accessed/Dirty (for page replacement algorithms). These hardware-enforced permissions create the security boundary between applications and the kernel.

keyConcepts.name: MMU
keyConcepts.description: Memory Management Unit. Hardware that translates virtual to physical addresses on every memory access.

keyConcepts.name: Page Table Entry (PTE)
keyConcepts.description: Contains physical frame number, permission bits, and status bits for one page mapping.

keyConcepts.name: TLB Miss
keyConcepts.description: When translation not in TLB. Requires slow page table walk.

keyConcepts.name: Segmentation Fault
keyConcepts.description: Program accessing invalid memory. OS kills program with SIGSEGV.

complexity.translation: O(1) with TLB hit, O(page_table_levels) with miss

steps.title: Split Virtual Address
steps.description: Divide virtual address into page number and offset components.

steps.title: TLB Lookup
steps.description: Check TLB for cached translation of virtual page number.

steps.title: Page Table Walk
steps.description: Traverse page table levels: PML4→PDPT→PD→PT to find PTE.

steps.title: Construct Physical Address
steps.description: Combine physical frame number from PTE with original offset.

practiceProblems.title: Virtual Memory Purpose
practiceProblems.description: What does virtual memory provide that physical memory doesn't?
practiceProblems.explanation: Virtual memory allows each process to have its own isolated address space with protection from other processes and controlled access permissions.

practiceProblems.title: Page Size
practiceProblems.description: What is the standard page size on most x86-64 systems?
practiceProblems.explanation: The standard page size is 4 KB (4096 bytes). Systems also support huge pages (2MB, 1GB) for large memory applications.

practiceProblems.title: TLB Function
practiceProblems.description: What is the purpose of the TLB?
practiceProblems.explanation: The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-to-physical translations to avoid slow page table walks on every access.

practiceProblems.title: Page Fault Cause
practiceProblems.description: When does a page fault occur?
practiceProblems.answer: Accessing a page not in physical memory
practiceProblems.explanation: Page faults occur when accessing a page not present in RAM—either swapped out to disk, not yet allocated, or invalid (causing segfault).

practiceProblems.title: Address Translation
practiceProblems.description: If virtual page 0x100 maps to physical frame 0x200 and offset is 0x500, what is the physical address?

practiceProblems.title: Page Table Levels
practiceProblems.description: Why do x86-64 systems use multi-level page tables instead of a single large table?
practiceProblems.answer: Save space for sparse address spaces
practiceProblems.explanation: Multi-level tables only allocate pages for used address regions. A single table for 64-bit addresses would require enormous memory (512GB for 4KB pages).

minigame.title: Virtual Voyager
minigame.description: Navigate the virtual memory system! Translate addresses, manage TLBs, handle page faults, and optimize memory access patterns. Master the art of address translation!
instructions: Virtual addresses appear and need translation
First check TLB for fast translation
On TLB miss, walk the page table
Handle page faults by allocating frames
Update page tables and TLB after translations
Minimize page table walks for best performance!

snippets.title: Virtual Memory Simulator
snippets.code:
class PageTableEntry:
    def __init__(self):
        self.present = False
        self.frame = 0
        self.read_write = True
        self.user_supervisor = True
        self.accessed = False
        self.dirty = False

class VirtualMemorySystem:
    def __init__(self, num_frames=16):
        self.num_frames = num_frames
        self.frames = [None] * num_frames  # None = free
        self.page_table = {}  # vpn -> PTE
        self.tlb = {}  # vpn -> (frame, access_count)
        self.tlb_accesses = 0
        self.tlb_hits = 0
        self.page_faults = 0
        self.page_size = 4096
    
    def get_vpn_offset(self, va):
        vpn = va // self.page_size
        offset = va % self.page_size
        return vpn, offset
    
    def tlb_lookup(self, vpn):
        self.tlb_accesses += 1
        if vpn in self.tlb:
            self.tlb_hits += 1
            frame, _ = self.tlb[vpn]
            return frame
        return None
    
    def tlb_update(self, vpn, frame):
        # Simple FIFO TLB
        if len(self.tlb) >= 8:
            oldest = min(self.tlb.keys(), key=lambda k: self.tlb[k][1])
            del self.tlb[oldest]
        self.tlb[vpn] = (frame, self.tlb_accesses)
    
    def allocate_frame(self):
        for i, frame in enumerate(self.frames):
            if frame is None:
                return i
        # Page replacement: simple FIFO
        victim = self.page_faults % self.num_frames
        # Would write back if dirty
        old_vpn = self.frames[victim]
        if old_vpn in self.page_table:
            self.page_table[old_vpn].present = False
        return victim
    
    def translate(self, va, is_write=False):
        vpn, offset = self.get_vpn_offset(va)
        
        # Check TLB first
        frame = self.tlb_lookup(vpn)
        if frame is not None:
            return (frame * self.page_size) + offset
        
        # TLB miss - check page table
        if vpn not in self.page_table:
            self.page_table[vpn] = PageTableEntry()
        
        pte = self.page_table[vpn]
        
        if not pte.present:
            # Page fault!
            self.page_faults += 1
            frame = self.allocate_frame()
            self.frames[frame] = vpn
            pte.present = True
            pte.frame = frame
        
        # Update access bits
        pte.accessed = True
        if is_write:
            pte.dirty = True
        
        # Update TLB
        self.tlb_update(vpn, pte.frame)
        
        return (pte.frame * self.page_size) + offset
    
    def get_stats(self):
        tlb_hit_rate = self.tlb_hits / self.tlb_accesses if self.tlb_accesses > 0 else 0
        return {
            'tlb_accesses': self.tlb_accesses,
            'tlb_hits': self.tlb_hits,
            'tlb_hit_rate': tlb_hit_rate,
            'page_faults': self.page_faults
        }

# Test
vm = VirtualMemorySystem(num_frames=4)

# Sequential access (good locality)
print('Sequential access:')
for i in range(8):
    addr = i * 4  # 4-byte words
    pa = vm.translate(addr)
    print(f'  VA 0x{addr:04X} -> PA 0x{pa:04X}')

stats = vm.get_stats()
print(f'\nTLB Hit Rate: {stats["tlb_hit_rate"]:.1%}')
print(f'Page Faults: {stats["page_faults"]}')

# Random access (poor locality)
vm2 = VirtualMemorySystem(num_frames=4)
print('\nRandom access:')
import random
for _ in range(8):
    addr = random.randint(0, 32) * 4
    pa = vm2.translate(addr)
    print(f'  VA 0x{addr:04X} -> PA 0x{pa:04X}')

stats2 = vm2.get_stats()
print(f'\nTLB Hit Rate: {stats2["tlb_hit_rate"]:.1%}')
print(f'Page Faults: {stats2["page_faults"]}')
